1.title: A Geological Upheaval 50 Million Years Ago
1.html:
Fifty million years ago the Vosges mountains and Germany's Black Forest (Forêt Noire) were a single massif. From the Tertiary onwards, the middle of this massif gradually sank, and over a long span of geological time formed today's Rhine plain (rift valley).

As a result, rock layers laid down in almost every geological period were exposed again along the edges of the fault zone — and Alsace's vineyards sit exactly on this fault zone. This is the fundamental reason why most Alsace wine villages have 4 or 5 completely different soil layers.

Two main fault lines form the skeleton of this land: the Vosges fault (the boundary of the crystalline massif) and the Rhine fault (beyond which lie the Rhine alluvial deposits).
2.title: Comparing the Three Landforms
2.items.0.label: A. Foothills (Rebord de la montagne)
2.items.0.desc: Mainly siliceous rock; drainage and sunshine are key. Altitude 250–360 m, slopes up to 65% (hence terracing), thin soils (about 30 cm, except for alluvial deposits at the foot). Crystalline rock and early sediments dominate in the south, while sandstone prevails in the north (around Saverne).
2.items.1.label: B. Sub-Vosges Hills (Collines sous-vosgiennes)
2.items.1.desc: Mainly limestone, the "climatic optimum" (optimum climatique). Altitude 200–360 m, slopes about 25%, deeper soils (0.5–2 m). Concentrated in a band from Dambach to Marlenheim, home to most of Alsace's top vineyards.
2.items.2.label: C. Rhine Alluvial Plain (Plaine alluviale du Rhin)
2.items.2.desc: Soil water-holding capacity is the key indicator — the strata are younger and less developed. Altitude 170–220 m, gentle slopes, deep and uniform soils, with good water properties from alluvial run-off and longer sunshine hours.
3.question: Why do many Alsace wine villages have 4 or 5 completely different soil layers?
3.options.1: Fifty million years ago the Vosges and Black Forest collapsed together, exposing rock layers of different geological ages along the fault zone — exactly where the vineyards sit
3.options.2: The Rhine changed course many times, bringing different sediments
3.options.3: It only happens in a few exceptional villages
3.explanation: Fifty million years ago the Vosges and Black Forest were one massif; from the Tertiary the middle sank and formed the Rhine plain. This crustal movement exposed rock layers of different ages along the fault zone, and Alsace's vineyards sit exactly on it, so most wine villages have several different soil layers — the basic starting point for understanding Alsace's terroir diversity.
4.keyPoints.0: The Vosges and Black Forest were once one; the Tertiary collapse formed today's Rhine plain (rift valley)
4.keyPoints.1: The Vosges and Rhine faults are the two key clues to Alsace geology
4.keyPoints.2: Three zones: foothills (siliceous rock, steep terraced slopes), sub-Vosges hills (limestone, climatic optimum), Rhine alluvial plain (water retention is key)
4.keyPoints.3: The sub-Vosges hills hold most of Alsace's top vineyards, concentrated between Dambach and Marlenheim
